A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Vlaser study and contain readable methods, results, figures, equations, and appendices. Renamed models and relocated appendix material can be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original embodied-reasoning evaluations and downstream WidowX and Google Robot experiments in Tables 1–3, with qualitative demonstrations in the appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains those results and adds RoboTwin evaluations, controlled ablations, and human reassessment of generated-data quality.

M1.justification: Appendix A.2 adds an explicit judge-and-filter stage to the described in-domain data pipeline: Qwen2.5VL-32B scores QA pairs, and score-1 samples are rejected. The InternVL3 backbone, flow-matching action expert, and two-stage training remain. The PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun with this filtering.

E1.justification: v2 adds evaluation on 12 RoboTwin tasks using the bimanual Aloha-AgileX embodiment and explicitly includes RoboTwin in its training-data sources. This substantially extends the previous SimplerEnv robot evaluations. v1 already contained an illustrative RoboTwin grounding sample in Figure 4, but no corresponding benchmark evaluation.

E2.justification: v2 adds RDT-1B as an evaluated comparator in RoboTwin Table 4. It also adds Spatial and Grounding variants to the WidowX comparison and Vlaser-All to both SimplerEnv tables. Existing external comparator sets in Tables 1–3 are retained; Vlaser-OOD matches the earlier Vlaser variant.

E3.justification: v2 introduces controlled prediction/execution-length and 10-versus-20 sampling-step experiments, plus a RoboTwin comparison with aligned 30k-step training. Section 2.3 corrects the integration step from 10 to 0.1, consistent with the previously documented ten inference steps. Reporting remains inconsistent: Section 3.3 and Table 5 use four executed actions by default, while Appendix A.1/A.3 still specify two.

E4.justification: v2 expands data-source ablations with WidowX Spatial/Grounding results and combined-data Vlaser-All experiments. New Section 3.3 tests sensitivity to action prediction length, execution length, and sampling steps. Appendix A.2 adds human validation of automated data-quality scores. The earlier qualitative rollout demonstrations are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports benchmark confidence intervals, repeated-training seed statistics, or significance tests. The new human–judge agreement percentage is an additional validation result, without an accompanying uncertainty estimate or changed uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial RoboTwin, data-mixture, and sensitivity results. Vlaser-All reports 65.1% on WidowX, 76.2%/59.0% on Google Robot visual matching/variant aggregation, and 67.5% on RoboTwin. These are new configurations, not same-setting improvements over v1. Table 2 corrects Vlaser-QA's average from 64.6% to 62.6% while retaining its task scores. Table 1's results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The explicit expectation added to Equation 2 and expanded observation/noise notation formalize the existing sampled flow-matching objective. They introduce no substantive new mathematical argument, theorem, proof, or formal assumption.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contributions, and conclusion retain the same central claims: the Vlaser model and dataset, analysis of data effectiveness for VLA transfer, leading embodied-reasoning/WidowX performance, and competitive Google Robot performance. The added experiments provide further support without redefining these contributions.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges the absence of real-robot experiments in its new limitations section. It also interprets combined in-domain data as beneficial for transfer and the new hyperparameter experiments as evidence of robustness. The central explanation based on visual observation domain shift is retained.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's generation instructions, v2 supplies the filtering judge, three scoring rubrics, rejection rule, complete filtering prompts, and human-check procedure. It also expands action-expert implementation explanations and documents RoboTwin's training budget. Existing hyperparameter tables largely remain. The new declaration that AI generated no research data conflicts with the LLM-based data generation described in Appendix A.2.

R1.justification: v2 adds targeted references for RoboTwin, RDT-1B, mixture-of-experts architecture, synthetic-data construction, and LLM judging, while retaining its central research positioning. It trims some broad criticism of existing VLAs. The revised open-pi-zero attribution and duplicate Shazeer entry do not represent distinct new prior works.

P1.justification: Editing is concentrated in the action-expert explanation and experimental discussion, including clearer Vlaser-OOD terminology. Ablation, limitations, ethics, reproducibility, and LLM-use sections are added, and the conference header changes. The abstract, introduction, conclusion, and substantial portions of the body remain essentially unchanged.

P2.justification: Figure 2 is substantially redrawn to explain token flow and robot outputs. Figure 1 revises the radar display and corrects robot labels. New RoboTwin and ablation tables accompany expanded Tables 2–3; Figures 3 and 5 gain RoboTwin examples. Appendix examples are rearranged, while Figures 6–7 retain their original demonstrations.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the central transfer argument through an additional bimanual embodiment, fuller data-mixture comparisons, and controlled action/sampling ablations, reducing reliance on one simulator and one configuration. The filtering documentation and explicit real-robot limitation also improve assessability. These gains outweigh the execution-length inconsistency and contradictory AI-use declaration, which remain material reporting weaknesses.
